input.query: Do the authors offer a hypothesis for why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country?

output.reason: The evidence supports a qualified answer. The Discussion section states that Twitter matches populations better when weighted by GDP (implying it represents wealthier/urban populations) and that Twitter has fewer missing languages than web data. The Population Demographics section offers a partial explanation: English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so countries predominantly using these languages are over-represented by default. However, the paper does not present a single explicit hypothesis specifically framed as explaining why Twitter yields a better language-inventory prediction; it provides these related observations (common-language over-representation, GDP/urban skew, fewer missing languages). Thus the evidence supports that authors offer factors/interpretations relevant to this, though not a neatly labeled hypothesis.

claims.text: The paper reports that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.
In cases where corpora fail to represent all census languages produced by local populations, the authors state that Twitter has fewer missing languages.
The authors note that Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania.
The authors explain that English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so any country predominantly using these two languages will have a good representation by default.

The authors observe that Twitter data matches populations better when population numbers are weighted by GDP and worse when weighted by internet-usage statistics, which they say implies Twitter as a platform represents more wealthy populations than general web-crawled data.
The authors offer an alternate interpretation that their Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have more wealthy populations.

The stated GDP/wealth and urban-area explanations are framed as reasons why Twitter and web-crawled data diverge in representing populations, rather than as an explicit hypothesis specifically explaining why Twitter better predicts each country's language inventory.
